Six books, one binding

Here’s something special. You may remember a blog I posted about dos-à-dos (or “back-to-back”) books. These are very special objects consisting of usually two books, which were bound together at their, well, backs. When you were done with the one book, you would flip the object and read the other. The dos-à-dos book you see here is even more special. Not only is it a rather old one (it was bound in the late 16th century), but it contains not two but six books, all neatly hidden inside a single binding (see this motionless pic to admire it). They are all devotional texts printed in Germany during the 1550s and 1570s (including Martin Luther, Der kleine Catechismus) and each one is closed with its own tiny clasp. While it may have been difficult to keep track of a particular text’s location, a book you can open in six different ways is quite the display of craftsmanship.

I've never questioned a fairly basic assumption with regard to the electronics in my truck (and in any other vehicle for that matter) until I made the mistake of thinking through it last night while tracking down a bad relay. Hopefully someone knows the answer to this and can explain it to me in simple words...

The battery has a large red wire that goes to, among other places, the starter, the fuse block, the alternator / regulator, and so on. The battery also has a large "plus" sign next to that particular terminal. We always called it the positive terminal.

The battery also has a large black wire that goes to the nearest metal contact points on the engine and body. The battery has a large "minus" sign next to that terminal. We always called it the negative terminal.

My understanding is this:

Electricity flows from the positive terminal to the various components in the vehicle. The various components are (usually) connected to something metal, either directly screwed in, or through a small short wire that is fastened to metal. As the electricity flows into the component, it is the voltage drop between the positive wire that is supplying the electricity, and the metal that eventually makes it back to the battery, that allow the component to function. That is, the component makes the electricity work to get back to the battery, and that work results in lights or motors or sound.

That much makes sense to me.

-=However=-

Electrons have a negative charge.

Does the electricity flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal? I don't like that as a solution, because it makes no sense to have the switches, controls, relays, etc, as the last part of a circuit.

So

Is the positive terminal the source of all of the negatively-charged electrons? In which case, isn't the +/- designation the opposite of what is actually going on in the battery?

Electricity flows out of the negative terminal and into the positive terminal. If that hurts the brain think about it like this. The wire had a fixed number of cups that can hold a single electron. They are all filled when there is no potential across the wire. When you connect a voltage difference across the wire the electron closest to the positive side moves out of the cup towards the positive potential. This leaves a cup open and the 2nd to last electron jumps over one cup. So now the 2nd cup is vacant. Looking just at the cups it looks like the cup has moved from the 1st to the 2nd position. Repeat this a few billion billion billion times and it looks like the cups are moving from the positive to the negative. When an electron moves to another atom it makes a positive ion so the positive charge is moving towards the negative.

Nothing really changes except the direction. It's why there's no need to change everything.

The reason for this confusion is because of Ben Franklin. He has a glass rod and an amber rod he would charge with fur. They were opposite polarity and he picked one to be positive and the other negative. 50/50 chance to get it right.

Yeah, electricity is strange because it came before particle physics. We gave the electrical potentials (+) and (-) symbols before we discovered the electron.

The electron being a negatively charged particle only gets stranger when you go further down the sciences because when we talk about "current flow" as amounts of charge, we're actually talking about amounts of electrons moving in the opposite direction. (Example: there is a potential of 5 volts across a resistor, and 1 ampere of current passing through it. Since we define the current as charge moving, a positive current means that electrons are moving in the opposite direction at a rate of 1 ampere.) The cup analogy by /u/bman0321 is one way of dealing with this problem to make the math work a little better.

As far as the reason for car and house wiring being different, I was always told it has to do with catalytic rust prevention. We call the car's frame its ground, but it helps prevent rusting if we give that frame a surplus of electrons. (Oxygen atoms are less likely to get near it, which makes rusting less likely to happen) So cars have their 'ground' charged by default, while house wiring have their ground actually grounded for safety.
